title: Mughal empire: emperors, administration and monuments
seo_title: Mughal Empire: Emperors, Administration and Monuments
meta_description: The Mughal empire from Babur to 1857: the six great emperors, the mansabdari system, decline after Aurangzeb, and the forts and tombs of Delhi and Agra.
summary: The Mughal empire was founded by Babur after the first battle of Panipat in 1526 and lasted, in name, until 1857. Under Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb it ruled most of the subcontinent. It is known for the mansabdari system, Persianate court culture, and monuments such as Humayun's Tomb, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort.

paras: Historians usually speak of the six great Mughals, from Babur to Aurangzeb. After 1707 the emperors continued at Delhi, but with shrinking real power.

sections.h2: From Babur to Akbar: building an empire
paras: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526 and the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527. His son Humayun lost the empire to the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri in 1540. Sher Shah, though he ruled for only five years, reorganised revenue, issued the silver rupiya and improved the road from Bengal to the north-west. Humayun returned in 1555 and died a year later after a fall on the stairs of the Sher Mandal in Purana Qila.

Akbar, who came to the throne at thirteen, won the second battle of Panipat in 1556 against Hemu. Over fifty years he brought Rajasthan, Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir and parts of the Deccan under control, often through alliances and marriages with Rajput rulers who were then given high rank.

sections.h2: Mughal administration: the mansabdari system and revenue
paras: The heart of Mughal government was the mansabdari system. Every officer, civil or military, held a mansab, a rank expressed in two numbers: zat (personal rank and pay) and sawar (the number of cavalry he had to maintain). Mansabdars were usually paid through jagirs, assignments of revenue from a territory, which were transferred regularly so that no noble built a local power base.

Revenue under Akbar was reorganised by his finance minister Raja Todar Mal. The zabt system measured land and fixed cash rates based on average yields and prices over ten years, a method called dahsala. Provinces (subas) were run by a governor (subadar), a finance officer (diwan) and other officials. Persian was the language of administration, and the Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl describes this system in detail.

Akbar abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564, held religious debates at the Ibadat Khana in Fatehpur Sikri, and promoted sulh-i kul, often translated as peace with all. Sanskrit texts including the Mahabharata were translated into Persian. Jahangir's reign was a high point for Mughal painting, with natural history studies and portraits. Shah Jahan's court favoured white marble, inlay and symmetry. Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679, and his religious policies remain much debated by historians.

Mughal buildings combine Persian and Central Asian planning with Indian craft. Our guide to [Mughal architecture](mughal-architecture.html) traces the line from [Humayun's Tomb](humayuns-tomb.html), the first great garden tomb in India, to the Taj Mahal.

The Mughal empire was one of the largest economies of its time. Indian cotton textiles, indigo and saltpetre were exported in large quantities, and silver from the Americas flowed in to pay for them. Surat in Gujarat was the main western port, and Hindustani merchants and bankers operated across the Indian Ocean.

European trading companies arrived in this setting. The English East India Company set up a factory at Surat in 1613, and Sir Thomas Roe came as ambassador of James I to Jahangir's court in 1615. The Dutch, French and Danes followed. For most of the 17th century these companies were minor players dependent on Mughal permission; their military and political power grew only as the empire weakened in the 18th century.

sections.h2: Why did the Mughal empire decline?
paras: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, wars of succession, the cost of the long Deccan campaigns, a shortage of good jagirs for the nobility (the jagirdari crisis), and the rise of regional powers such as the Marathas, the Sikhs, Hyderabad, Awadh and Bengal all weakened the centre. Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 and carried off the Peacock Throne.

By the late 18th century the emperor ruled little beyond Delhi, under Maratha and then British protection. The last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was made the symbolic leader of the Revolt of 1857 and was exiled to Rangoon in 1858.

sections.h2: Mughal monuments in Delhi and Agra
paras: Delhi has the Mughal story from beginning to end: Humayun's Dinpanah at [Purana Qila](purana-qila.html), Humayun's Tomb, Shah Jahan's [Red Fort complex](red-fort-complex.html) and Jama Masjid, and the last Mughal summer palace, Zafar Mahal, in Mehrauli. Agra and Fatehpur Sikri hold Akbar's and Shah Jahan's capitals; our [Fatehpur Sikri visit](fatehpur-sikri-mughal-urban-vision.html) reads the city as a plan. The [Golden Triangle with an archaeologist](the-golden-triangle-with-an-archaeologist.html) links all three cities.

faq.q: Who was the founder of the Mughal empire?
faq.a: Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana in Central Asia and ruler of Kabul, founded the Mughal empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the first battle of Panipat in 1526. He descended from Timur on his father's side and from Chinggis Khan on his mother's.

The mansabdari system, organised under Akbar, gave every officer a numerical rank (mansab) with two parts: zat for personal status and salary, and sawar for the cavalry he had to maintain. Mansabdars were usually paid through transferable revenue assignments called jagirs.

faq.q: Who was the last Mughal emperor?
faq.a: Bahadur Shah Zafar (Bahadur Shah II) was the last Mughal emperor. He was proclaimed leader by rebel soldiers in 1857, tried by the British after Delhi was retaken, and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862.

faq.q: Which is the first Mughal monument built in India?
faq.a: Babur commissioned mosques at Panipat, Sambhal and Ayodhya and laid out gardens at Agra. The first monumental Mughal building in the full sense is usually taken to be Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, completed in the early 1570s and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faq.q: When did the Mughal empire reach its largest size?
faq.a: Under Aurangzeb, in the late 17th century, after the annexation of the Bijapur and Golconda sultanates in 1686 and 1687. The empire then stretched from Kabul to the far south, though control over the Deccan was never secure.

posts.hook: Humayun died after a fall on a library staircase.
posts.caption: In 1556, a year after regaining Delhi, he slipped on the steep stairs of the Sher Mandal in Purana Qila. The building still stands.

posts.hook: See Humayun's Tomb before the Taj Mahal.
posts.caption: The garden plan, double dome and raised platform all appear first at Humayun's Tomb. Seeing it first makes the Taj make more sense.
